title: Charlie and the Great Glass Elevator
author: Roald Dahl
short_summary: Charlie Bucket, his whole family and Willy Wonka soar into space in the Great Glass Elevator after it shoots straight through the roof of the chocolate factory. They dock with an orbiting Space Hotel, survive an encounter with the shape-shifting Vermicious Knids, and return to Earth — where Wonka's youth pills cause a second disaster in the family's own bedroom, and Charlie has to help rescue a grandmother who has vanished altogether.
extended_summary:
The Great Glass Elevator goes up so hard that it leaves the atmosphere, carrying Charlie, his parents, Grandpa Joe, and the bed containing the three grandparents who still refuse to get out of it. Far below, the world's first Space Hotel is being opened, and the arrival of an unidentified glass box on the radar causes panic in Washington. Wonka docks with the hotel anyway — and finds it already occupied by Vermicious Knids, shape-shifting creatures who can twist themselves into any form, including letters that spell out a message. Wonka gets everyone away, tows the trapped hotel staff home behind the elevator, and the Knids clinging on burn up when they hit the Earth's atmosphere.

Back at the factory, the trouble starts again. Wonka has invented Wonka-Vite, which takes twenty years off you per pill. The three grandparents take far too many: Grandpa George and Grandma Josephine turn into babies, and Grandma Georgina, who was seventy-eight, goes right past zero to minus two and disappears into Minusland. Charlie goes with Wonka in the elevator to find her, sprays her with Vita-Wonk — the opposite invention, which makes you older — and brings her back at the age of three hundred and fifty-eight.

A carefully measured dose of Wonka-Vite brings everyone back to sensible ages. The book ends with a letter from the President inviting them all to the White House, at which the three grandparents leap out of the bed they have not left in twenty years.

questions.prompt: While Charlie's family are still in the elevator, what is happening down on Earth that makes their arrival in orbit so alarming?

options: A new Space Hotel is being opened with great ceremony
A rocket is about to be launched from the same spot
A meteor shower has been forecast for that same day
A total eclipse has left the tracking stations blind

questions.explanation: The Americans are opening the world's first Space Hotel, and an unidentified glass box on the radar is assumed to be an enemy attack. Half the comedy of the book comes from this misunderstanding: the President's men treat a chocolate maker's lift as an international emergency.

questions.prompt: Why can the Vermicious Knids not simply follow the elevator back down to Earth?

options: They burn up when they hit the atmosphere
They cannot survive without the hotel's air
They are too heavy to fall at the right speed
They will not go anywhere sunlight can reach

questions.explanation: The Knids that cling on are destroyed by the heat of re-entry, exactly as a meteor would be. It is one of the places where Dahl quietly does real science in the middle of nonsense — the elevator survives because Wonka has planned for it, and the Knids have not.

questions.prompt: Each pill of Wonka-Vite takes exactly ___ years off the age of whoever swallows it.
questions.explanation: That single number is what makes the disaster arithmetic work: Grandma Georgina, who is seventy-eight, swallows four pills, loses eighty years and ends up at minus two. Dahl lets the reader do the sum before the characters do.

questions.prompt: What happens to Grandpa George and Grandma Josephine when they take too much Wonka-Vite?

options: They turn into babies
They fall into a deep sleep
They shrink but stay grown up
They lose their memories entirely

questions.explanation: Two elderly people who have spent the whole book complaining from a bed become infants who have to be carried. The joke has a point: they wanted to be young again and had no idea what they were actually asking for.

questions.prompt: Put the events of the story in the order they happen.

items: The elevator goes so high that it leaves the Earth behind
The travellers dock with the orbiting Space Hotel
The Knids that follow them down burn up on re-entry
The three grandparents swallow too much Wonka-Vite
Charlie and Wonka go down into Minusland
A letter arrives inviting the family to the White House

questions.explanation: The book is really two adventures joined in the middle: a space story and a story about ageing. The hinge is the return home, and Dahl makes the second half the more frightening one — the danger is now inside the family's own bedroom.

questions.prompt: Match each invention or creature to what it does.

right: Removes twenty years from you with every pill
Adds years on, and can be sprayed at someone
Can twist into any shape, including letters
The grey place where those of minus age are

questions.explanation: Dahl builds the second half around a perfectly balanced pair of inventions: one subtracts years, one adds them, and the plot is the arithmetic of getting from one to the other. Minusland is where you land if the subtraction goes too far.

questions.prompt: Sort each event by which half of the book it belongs to.

options.label: The travellers dock with a brand-new hotel
Shape-shifting creatures form themselves into letters
A capsule full of staff is towed home on a rope
Two old people turn into babies in a bed
A grandmother is sprayed to make her older
The elevator travels down instead of up

questions.explanation: The two halves mirror each other. Both begin with Wonka's invention being used carelessly by somebody else, both put Charlie's family in real danger, and in both cases the way out is Wonka knowing one precise fact that nobody else does.

questions.prompt: Grandma Georgina disappears completely instead of just becoming young. Why does that happen to her and not to the others?

options: Her dose took her past zero to a minus age
She swallowed hers before the others did
She was the oldest person in the whole family
She took hers without any water to wash it down

questions.explanation: Four pills took eighty years off a woman of seventy-eight, and there is nothing at the bottom of that sum but minus two. Dahl treats his own invented rule seriously and follows it wherever it goes, which is exactly why Minusland has to exist.

questions.prompt: Mr. Wonka invents things that are wonderful and dangerous at the same time — a lift that flies into space, a pill that makes you younger. Should he be allowed to keep inventing whatever he likes? Give your reasons.
questions.explanation: Both sides can earn full marks. A strong 'yes' answer notices that Wonka is also the only person who can undo the damage, and that the grandparents took the pills against his warnings. A strong 'no' answer notices that a grandmother ceased to exist, that people nearly died in orbit, and that Wonka enjoys the danger rather more than he should. Accept either, argued from the book.

questions.prompt: Wonka's two inventions are exact opposites: one takes years away, the other puts them back. Invent a pair of Wonka sweets that work as opposites in the same way. What would each one do, and what would go wrong if somebody took too much of one?
questions.explanation: There is no single right answer. A strong answer invents two genuinely opposite effects and then, like Dahl, follows the rule past the point where it stops being funny — the 'what goes wrong' half is the part that shows the child understood how the book works.

questions.prompt: To bring Grandma Georgina back, Wonka uses the opposite of his youth pills — a liquid called ___, which makes a person older.
questions.explanation: It is sprayed rather than swallowed, which is how they can use it on somebody who is not really there. The dose is a guess, and it overshoots: Georgina comes back at three hundred and fifty-eight years old.

questions.prompt: At the very end of the book, what finally gets the three grandparents out of the bed they have refused to leave?

options: An invitation to visit the President
A promise of more Wonka-Vite pills
A second trip in the glass elevator
The news that the factory is closing

questions.explanation: After surviving space, infancy and Minusland, what actually gets them up is a letter from the White House. Dahl's last joke is that people who would not move for anything will move for a grand enough invitation.
